claim: TB is the most common illness in HIV-1-infected individuals.
source: Indeed, TB is the most common illness in HIV-1-infected individuals, about 55% of TB notified patients are also infected with HIV-1, and about a fifth of the TB death toll occurs in HIV-1 co-infected individuals (WHO health report 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to WHO health report 2017.

claim: About 55% of TB notified patients are also infected with HIV-1.
source: Indeed, TB is the most common illness in HIV-1-infected individuals, about 55% of TB notified patients are also infected with HIV-1, and about a fifth of the TB death toll occurs in HIV-1 co-infected individuals (WHO health report 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to WHO health report 2017.

claim: About a fifth of the TB death toll occurs in HIV-1 co-infected individuals.
source: Indeed, TB is the most common illness in HIV-1-infected individuals, about 55% of TB notified patients are also infected with HIV-1, and about a fifth of the TB death toll occurs in HIV-1 co-infected individuals (WHO health report 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to WHO health report 2017.

claim: Clinical studies evidence a synergy between Mtb and HIV-1, which is associated with a spectrum of aberration in immune function.
source: Clinical studies evidence a synergy between these two pathogens, which is associated with a spectrum of aberration in immune function (Esmail et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Esmail et al., 2018.

claim: The mechanisms by which Mtb exacerbates HIV-1 infection require further investigation.
source: Yet, while progress has been made towards understanding how HIV-1 enhances Mtb growth and spread, the mechanisms by which Mtb exacerbates HIV-1 infection require further investigation (Bell and Noursadeghi, 2018; Deffur et al., 2013; Diedrich and Flynn, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bell and Noursadeghi, 2018; Deffur et al., 2013; Diedrich and Flynn, 2011.

claim: Macrophages are infected by HIV-1 in humans and by SIV in non-human primates.
source: Besides CD4+ T cells, macrophages are infected by HIV-1 in humans and by the simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV), the most closely related lentivirus to HIV, in non-human primates (NHP) (Cribbs et al., 2015; Rodrigues et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cribbs et al., 2015; Rodrigues et al., 2017.

claim: Macrophages sustain HIV-1 infection and replication, even in the absence of T cells.
source: Recently, using a humanized mouse model, macrophages were shown to sustain HIV-1 infection and replication, even in the absence of T cells (Honeycutt et al., 2017; Honeycutt et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Honeycutt et al., 2017; Honeycutt et al., 2016.

claim: Tissue macrophages, such as alveolar, microglia and gut macrophages, are reservoirs in HIV-1 patients undergoing antiretroviral therapy.
source: This is in line with several studies characterizing tissue macrophages, such as alveolar, microglia and gut macrophages, as reservoirs in HIV-1 patients undergoing antiretroviral therapy (Ganor et al., 2019; Jambo et al., 2014; Mathews et al., 2019; Sattentau and Stevenson, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ganor et al., 2019; Jambo et al., 2014; Mathews et al., 2019; Sattentau and Stevenson, 2016.

claim: Macrophages are key host cells for Mtb.
source: Macrophages are key host cells for Mtb (O'Garra et al., 2013; VanderVen et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to O'Garra et al., 2013; VanderVen et al., 2016.

claim: TB-associated microenvironments activate macrophages towards an M(IL-10) profile, distinguished by a CD16+CD163+MerTK+ phenotype.
source: Using relevant in vitro and in vivo models, we showed that TB-associated microenvironments activate macrophages towards an M(IL-10) profile, distinguished by a CD16+CD163+MerTK+ phenotype.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Souriant et al., 2019 and the authors' previous work.

claim: Acquisition of the M(IL-10) phenotype is dependent on the IL-10/STAT3 signaling pathway.
source: Acquisition of this phenotype is dependent on the IL-10/STAT3 signaling pathway (Lastrucci et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lastrucci et al., 2015.

claim: M(IL-10) macrophages are highly susceptible to Mtb infection.
source: M(IL-10) macrophages are highly susceptible not only to Mtb infection (Lastrucci et al., 2015), but also to HIV-1 infection and spread (Souriant et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lastrucci et al., 2015.

claim: M(IL-10) macrophages are highly susceptible to HIV-1 infection and spread.
source: M(IL-10) macrophages are highly susceptible not only to Mtb infection (Lastrucci et al., 2015), but also to HIV-1 infection and spread (Souriant et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Souriant et al., 2019.

claim: TB-associated microenvironments stimulate the formation of tunneling nanotubes (TNT).
source: At the functional level, we demonstrated that TB-associated microenvironments stimulate the formation of tunneling nanotubes (TNT), membranous channels connecting two or more cells over short to long distances above substrate.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Souriant et al., 2019 and the authors' previous work.

claim: Thick TNT are functionally distinguished by the transfer of large organelles, such as lysosomes and mitochondria.
source: Thick TNT are functionally distinguished by the transfer of large organelles, such as lysosomes and mitochondria (Dupont et al., 2018; Eugenin et al., 2009; Hashimoto et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dupont et al., 2018; Eugenin et al., 2009; Hashimoto et al., 2016.

claim: Total inhibition of TNT formation in M(IL-10) macrophages resulted in the abrogation of HIV-1 exacerbation induced by Mtb.
source: While the contribution for each TNT class to HIV-1 pathogenesis has not been explored (Dupont et al., 2018; Eugenin et al., 2009; Hashimoto et al., 2016), we reported that total inhibition of TNT formation in M(IL-10) macrophages resulted in the abrogation of HIV-1 exacerbation induced by Mtb (Souriant et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Souriant et al., 2019.

claim: Factors influencing TNT function in M(IL-10) macrophages remain unknown at large.
source: Factors influencing TNT function in M(IL-10) macrophages remain unknown at large.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Global mapping of the M(IL-10) macrophage transcriptome revealed Siglec-1 as a potential factor responsible for HIV-1 dissemination in the co-infection context with TB.
source: In this study, global mapping of the M(IL-10) macrophage transcriptome revealed Siglec-1 (CD169, or sialoadhesin) as a potential factor responsible for HIV-1 dissemination in the co-infection context with TB.
evidence: This claim is based on the transcriptomic analysis performed in this study.

claim: Siglec-1 is a type-I transmembrane lectin receptor.
source: As a type-I transmembrane lectin receptor, Siglec-1 possesses a large extracellular domain composed of 17 immunoglobulin-like domains, including the N-terminal V-set domain, which allows the trans recognition of terminal α2,3-linked sialic acid residues in O- and N-linked glycans and glycolipids, such as those surface-exposed in HIV-1 and SIV particles (Izquierdo-Useros et al., 2012a; Puryear et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Siglec-1 structure.

claim: Siglec-1 possesses a large extracellular domain composed of 17 immunoglobulin-like domains, including the N-terminal V-set domain.
source: As a type-I transmembrane lectin receptor, Siglec-1 possesses a large extracellular domain composed of 17 immunoglobulin-like domains, including the N-terminal V-set domain, which allows the trans recognition of terminal α2,3-linked sialic acid residues in O- and N-linked glycans and glycolipids, such as those surface-exposed in HIV-1 and SIV particles (Izquierdo-Useros et al., 2012a; Puryear et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Siglec-1 structure.

claim: The N-terminal V-set domain of Siglec-1 allows the trans recognition of terminal α2,3-linked sialic acid residues in O- and N-linked glycans and glycolipids.
source: As a type-I transmembrane lectin receptor, Siglec-1 possesses a large extracellular domain composed of 17 immunoglobulin-like domains, including the N-terminal V-set domain, which allows the trans recognition of terminal α2,3-linked sialic acid residues in O- and N-linked glycans and glycolipids, such as those surface-exposed in HIV-1 and SIV particles (Izquierdo-Useros et al., 2012a; Puryear et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Izquierdo-Useros et al., 2012a; Puryear et al., 2012.

claim: Terminal α2,3-linked sialic acid residues are surface-exposed in HIV-1 and SIV particles.
source: As a type-I transmembrane lectin receptor, Siglec-1 possesses a large extracellular domain composed of 17 immunoglobulin-like domains, including the N-terminal V-set domain, which allows the trans recognition of terminal α2,3-linked sialic acid residues in O- and N-linked glycans and glycolipids, such as those surface-exposed in HIV-1 and SIV particles (Izquierdo-Useros et al., 2012a; Puryear et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Izquierdo-Useros et al., 2012a; Puryear et al., 2012.

claim: Siglec-1 is clearly involved in the pathogenesis of HIV-1, SIV and other retroviruses.
source: While Siglec-1 has yet to be implicated in the TB context, it is clearly involved in the pathogenesis of HIV-1, SIV and other retroviruses (Martinez-Picado et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Martinez-Picado et al., 2017.

claim: Siglec-1 is mainly expressed in myeloid cells (e.g. macrophages and dendritic cells).
source: Siglec-1 is mainly expressed in myeloid cells (e.g. macrophages and dendritic cells) and participates in HIV-1 transfer from myeloid cells to T cells, as well as in the initiation of virus-containing compartment (VCC) formation in macrophages (Izquierdo-Useros et al., 2012a; Izquierdo-Useros et al., 2012b; Puryear et al., 2013; Puryear et al., 2012), and in the viral dissemination in vivo (Akiyama et al., 2017; Izquierdo-Useros et al., 2012a; Sewald et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Siglec-1 expression.

claim: Siglec-1 participates in HIV-1 transfer from myeloid cells to T cells.
source: Siglec-1 is mainly expressed in myeloid cells (e.g. macrophages and dendritic cells) and participates in HIV-1 transfer from myeloid cells to T cells, as well as in the initiation of virus-containing compartment (VCC) formation in macrophages (Izquierdo-Useros et al., 2012a; Izquierdo-Useros et al., 2012b; Puryear et al., 2013; Puryear et al., 2012), and in the viral dissemination in vivo (Akiyama et al., 2017; Izquierdo-Useros et al., 2012a; Sewald et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Izquierdo-Useros et al., 2012a; Izquierdo-Useros et al., 2012b; Puryear et al., 2013; Puryear et al., 2012.

claim: Siglec-1 participates in the initiation of virus-containing compartment (VCC) formation in macrophages.
source: Siglec-1 is mainly expressed in myeloid cells (e.g. macrophages and dendritic cells) and participates in HIV-1 transfer from myeloid cells to T cells, as well as in the initiation of virus-containing compartment (VCC) formation in macrophages (Izquierdo-Useros et al., 2012a; Izquierdo-Useros et al., 2012b; Puryear et al., 2013; Puryear et al., 2012), and in the viral dissemination in vivo (Akiyama et al., 2017; Izquierdo-Useros et al., 2012a; Sewald et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Izquierdo-Useros et al., 2012a; Izquierdo-Useros et al., 2012b; Puryear et al., 2013; Puryear et al., 2012.

claim: Siglec-1 participates in viral dissemination in vivo.
source: Siglec-1 is mainly expressed in myeloid cells (e.g. macrophages and dendritic cells) and participates in HIV-1 transfer from myeloid cells to T cells, as well as in the initiation of virus-containing compartment (VCC) formation in macrophages (Izquierdo-Useros et al., 2012a; Izquierdo-Useros et al., 2012b; Puryear et al., 2013; Puryear et al., 2012), and in the viral dissemination in vivo (Akiyama et al., 2017; Izquierdo-Useros et al., 2012a; Sewald et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Akiyama et al., 2017; Izquierdo-Useros et al., 2012a; Sewald et al., 2015.

claim: HIV-1 and other retroviruses have evolved the capacity to hijack the immune surveillance and housekeeping immunoregulatory functions of Siglec-1.
source: Indeed, HIV-1 and other retroviruses have evolved the capacity to hijack the immune surveillance and housekeeping immunoregulatory functions of Siglec-1 (Izquierdo-Useros et al., 2014; O'Neill et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Izquierdo-Useros et al., 2014; O'Neill et al., 2013.

claim: A distinct 60 gene-transcript signature was defined in cmMTB-treated cells.
source: A distinct 60 gene-transcript signature was defined in cmMTB-treated cells, using a combination of the expression level, statistical filters and hierarchical clustering; 51 genes were up-regulated and nine genes were down-regulated in cmMTB- compared to cmCTR-treated cells (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is based on the transcriptomic analysis performed in this study and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: 51 genes were up-regulated in cmMTB- compared to cmCTR-treated cells.
source: A distinct 60 gene-transcript signature was defined in cmMTB-treated cells, using a combination of the expression level, statistical filters and hierarchical clustering; 51 genes were up-regulated and nine genes were down-regulated in cmMTB- compared to cmCTR-treated cells (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is based on the transcriptomic analysis performed in this study and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Nine genes were down-regulated in cmMTB- compared to cmCTR-treated cells.
source: A distinct 60 gene-transcript signature was defined in cmMTB-treated cells, using a combination of the expression level, statistical filters and hierarchical clustering; 51 genes were up-regulated and nine genes were down-regulated in cmMTB- compared to cmCTR-treated cells (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is based on the transcriptomic analysis performed in this study and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: A significant fraction of genes that were up-regulated in response to interferon type I and II were also found significantly up-regulated in cmMTB-treated cells in comparison to control samples.
source: As shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, a significant fraction of genes that were up-regulated in response to interferon (IFN) type I (e.g. IFNα) and II (i.e. IFNγ), were also found, as a group, significantly up-regulated in cmMTB-treated cells in comparison to control samples (FDR q-value:<10-3).
evidence: This claim is based on GSEA analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Siglec-1 was up-regulated 7.4-fold in cmMTB-treated cells with an adjusted p-value of 0.0162.
source: However, among this ISG signature, the up-regulation of Siglec-1 (7.4-fold, adjusted p-value of 0.0162) in cmMTB-treated cells captured our attention due to its known role in HIV-1 pathogenesis (Izquierdo-Useros et al., 2014; O'Neill et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is based on the transcriptomic analysis performed in this study.

claim: High Siglec-1 expression was confirmed in cmMTB-treated macrophages at the mRNA level.
source: We confirmed a high Siglec-1 expression in cmMTB-treated macrophages at the mRNA (Figure 1B), intracellular and cell-surface protein (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–D) levels.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental validation shown in Figure 1B.

claim: High Siglec-1 expression was confirmed in cmMTB-treated macrophages at the intracellular protein level.
source: We confirmed a high Siglec-1 expression in cmMTB-treated macrophages at the mRNA (Figure 1B), intracellular and cell-surface protein (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–D) levels.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental validation shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–D.

claim: High Siglec-1 expression was confirmed in cmMTB-treated macrophages at the cell-surface protein level.
source: We confirmed a high Siglec-1 expression in cmMTB-treated macrophages at the mRNA (Figure 1B), intracellular and cell-surface protein (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–D) levels.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental validation shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–D.

claim: The effect of cmMTB on Siglec-1 expression was superior to the level obtained in HIV-1-infected cells.
source: This effect was superior to the level obtained in HIV-1-infected cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: cmMTB-treated macrophages displayed high density of Siglec-1 surface expression.
source: Particularly, cmMTB-treated macrophages displayed high density of Siglec-1 surface expression applying a quantitative FACS assay that determines the absolute number of Siglec-1 antibody binding sites per cell (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is based on quantitative FACS assay shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Siglec-1+ alveolar macrophages are present in lung biopsies of healthy non-human primates.
source: Histological immuno-staining confirmed the presence of Siglec-1+ alveolar macrophages in the lungs of healthy NHP (Figure 1E–F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), and revealed its significant increase in NHP mono-infected with either Mtb or SIV (Figure 1E–F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is based on histological analysis shown in Figure 1E–F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Siglec-1+ alveolar macrophages significantly increase in NHP mono-infected with either Mtb or SIV.
source: Histological immuno-staining confirmed the presence of Siglec-1+ alveolar macrophages in the lungs of healthy NHP (Figure 1E–F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), and revealed its significant increase in NHP mono-infected with either Mtb or SIV (Figure 1E–F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is based on histological analysis shown in Figure 1E–F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: There is a massive abundance of Siglec-1+ alveolar macrophages in co-infected NHP.
source: Strikingly, we noticed a massive abundance of these cells in co-infected NHP (Figure 1E–F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is based on histological analysis shown in Figure 1E–F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: There is a significant increase in the overall abundance of Siglec-1+ leukocytes in lungs of all infected NHP in comparison to healthy.
source: Concerning the overall abundance of Siglec-1+ leukocytes in lungs, we observed a significant increase in all infected NHP in comparison to healthy, with a higher tendency in active TB or co-infected NHP (Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is based on quantification shown in Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The number of Siglec-1+ leukocytes correlated positively with the severity of NHP pathology.
source: In fact, the number of Siglec-1+ leukocytes correlated positively with the severity of NHP pathology (Figure 1H, Supplementary file 1-Table S2).
evidence: This claim is based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 1H and Supplementary file 1-Table S2.

claim: Siglec-1+ cells were identified as alveolar macrophages based on their cell morphology, localization in alveoli, and co-expression with the macrophage marker CD163.
source: Based on their cell morphology, localization in alveoli, and co-expression with the macrophage marker CD163 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C), Siglec-1+ cells were identified as alveolar macrophages.
evidence: This claim is based on morphological and immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: Siglec-1 is up-regulated in alveolar macrophages in the context of a retroviral co-infection with active TB.
source: Collectively, these data show that Siglec-1 is up-regulated in alveolar macrophages in the context of a retroviral co-infection with active TB.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the data presented in the Results section.

claim: Siglec-1 is an ISG whose expression is induced by IFN-I in myeloid cells.
source: Siglec-1 is an ISG whose expression is induced by IFN-I in myeloid cells (Hartnell et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hartnell et al., 2001.

claim: IFN-I is induced in TB and known to mainly play a detrimental role.
source: In addition to viral infection, IFN-I is also induced in TB and known to mainly play a detrimental role (McNab et al., 2015; Moreira-Teixeira et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to McNab et al., 2015; Moreira-Teixeira et al., 2018.

claim: cmMTB contains high amounts of IFN-I compared to cmCTR.
source: First, we found that cmMTB contains high amounts of IFN-I compared to cmCTR (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is based on measurement shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Recombinant IFN-β significantly increased Siglec-1 cell-surface expression in macrophages, close to the level induced by cmMTB.
source: Next, we showed that recombinant IFN-β significantly increased Siglec-1 cell-surface expression in macrophages, close to the level induced by cmMTB (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: IL-10 modestly but significantly induced Siglec-1 expression in macrophages.
source: Interestingly, we observed a modest, albeit significant, induction of Siglec-1 expression in cells treated with interleukin 10 (IL-10), a cytokine we have previously shown to be abundant in cmMTB (Lastrucci et al., 2015) and that renders macrophages highly susceptible to HIV-1 infection (Souriant et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental observation and citations to Lastrucci et al., 2015 and Souriant et al., 2019.

claim: IL-10 depletion had no effect on Siglec-1 expression by cmMTB-treated cells.
source: However, IL-10 depletion had no effect on Siglec-1 expression by cmMTB-treated cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Blocking the IFN-I receptor (IFNAR-2) during cmMTB treatment fully abolished the expression of Siglec-1.
source: By contrast, blocking the IFN-I receptor (IFNAR-2) during cmMTB treatment fully abolished the expression of Siglec-1 (Figure 2D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), indicating that IFN-I is the responsible factor for Siglec-1 up-regulation in cmMTB-treated cells.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: IFN-I is the responsible factor for Siglec-1 up-regulation in cmMTB-treated cells.
source: By contrast, blocking the IFN-I receptor (IFNAR-2) during cmMTB treatment fully abolished the expression of Siglec-1 (Figure 2D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), indicating that IFN-I is the responsible factor for Siglec-1 up-regulation in cmMTB-treated cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the blocking experiment shown in Figure 2D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: IFN-I binding to IFNAR leads to the phosphorylation and nuclear translocation of the transcription factor STAT1.
source: IFN-I binding to IFNAR leads to the phosphorylation and nuclear translocation of the transcription factor STAT1, whose role is essential for transcription of ISG (Ivashkiv and Donlin, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ivashkiv and Donlin, 2014.

claim: STAT1 role is essential for transcription of ISG.
source: IFN-I binding to IFNAR leads to the phosphorylation and nuclear translocation of the transcription factor STAT1, whose role is essential for transcription of ISG (Ivashkiv and Donlin, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ivashkiv and Donlin, 2014.

claim: Zones rich in Siglec-1+ leukocytes also exhibited positivity for nuclear phosphorylated STAT1 (pSTAT1) in co-infected NHP lungs.
source: Histological staining of serial sections of co-infected lungs revealed that zones rich in Siglec-1+ leukocytes also exhibited positivity for nuclear phosphorylated STAT1 (pSTAT1) (Figure 2E), and the abundance of these two markers strongly correlated with the active status of TB in the different NHP groups (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is based on histological analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The abundance of Siglec-1+ leukocytes and pSTAT1+ cells strongly correlated with the active status of TB in the different NHP groups.
source: Histological staining of serial sections of co-infected lungs revealed that zones rich in Siglec-1+ leukocytes also exhibited positivity for nuclear phosphorylated STAT1 (pSTAT1) (Figure 2E), and the abundance of these two markers strongly correlated with the active status of TB in the different NHP groups (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The majority of Siglec-1+ alveolar macrophages were also positive for nuclear pSTAT1 in the infected NHP groups compared to healthy.
source: Moreover, we found that the majority of Siglec-1+ alveolar macrophages were also positive for nuclear pSTAT1 in the infected NHP groups compared to healthy (Figure 2E and G).
evidence: This claim is based on histological analysis shown in Figure 2E and G.

claim: There was a higher number of pSTAT1+ alveolar macrophages in TB-SIV co-infected lungs when compared to those from mono-infected NHP.
source: In fact, there was a higher number of pSTAT1+ alveolar macrophages in TB-SIV co-infected lungs when compared to those from mono-infected NHP and this number directly correlates with the number of Siglec-1+ alveolar macrophages (Figure 2G–H).
evidence: This claim is based on quantification shown in Figure 2G–H.

claim: The number of pSTAT1+ alveolar macrophages directly correlates with the number of Siglec-1+ alveolar macrophages.
source: In fact, there was a higher number of pSTAT1+ alveolar macrophages in TB-SIV co-infected lungs when compared to those from mono-infected NHP and this number directly correlates with the number of Siglec-1+ alveolar macrophages (Figure 2G–H).
evidence: This claim is based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 2G–H.

claim: Siglec-1 expression in human macrophages is controlled by IFN-I in a TB-associated microenvironment.
source: Altogether, these data demonstrate that Siglec-1 expression in human macrophages is controlled by IFN-I in a TB-associated microenvironment, and suggest the involvement of the IFN-I/STAT1/Siglec-1 axis in the pathogenesis of TB and co-infection with retroviruses.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the data presented in the Results section.

claim: The IFN-I/STAT1/Siglec-1 axis is involved in the pathogenesis of TB and co-infection with retroviruses.
source: Altogether, these data demonstrate that Siglec-1 expression in human macrophages is controlled by IFN-I in a TB-associated microenvironment, and suggest the involvement of the IFN-I/STAT1/Siglec-1 axis in the pathogenesis of TB and co-infection with retroviruses.
evidence: This is a suggestion based on the data presented in the Results section.

claim: TNT formation is responsible for the increase in HIV-1 spread between human macrophages in TB-associated microenvironments.
source: TNT formation is responsible for the increase in HIV-1 spread between human macrophages in TB-associated microenvironments (Souriant et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Souriant et al., 2019.

claim: Siglec-1 is localized mainly on microtubule (MT)-positive thick TNT, and not on thin TNT.
source: We observed that Siglec-1 is localized mainly on microtubule (MT)-positive thick TNT, and not on thin TNT (Figure 3A and Figure 3—video 1).
evidence: This claim is based on immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—video 1.

claim: About 50% of thick TNT were positive for Siglec-1.
source: Semi-automatic quantification of hundreds of TNT showed that about 50% of thick TNT were positive for Siglec-1 (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is based on quantification shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Siglec-1+ thick TNT exhibited a greater length compared to those lacking Siglec-1.
source: These TNT exhibited a greater length compared to those lacking Siglec-1 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is based on quantification shown in Figure 3C.

claim: HIV-1 viral proteins are found mainly inside Siglec-1+ thick TNT.
source: Importantly, unlike thin TNT, HIV-1 viral proteins are found mainly inside Siglec-1+ thick TNT (Figure 3D–E and Figure 3—video 2).
evidence: This claim is based on immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 3D–E and Figure 3—video 2.

claim: Siglec-1+ thick TNT also contained large organelles such as mitochondria.
source: In addition, these thick TNT also contained large organelles such as mitochondria (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), another characteristic distinguishing thick from thin TNT (Dupont et al., 2018; Onfelt et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is based on immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, and supported by citations to Dupont et al., 2018; Onfelt et al., 2006.

claim: The incidence of Siglec-1+ thick TNT between HIV-1 infected macrophages persisted for more than one week upon HIV-1 infection.
source: In general, we also noticed that the incidence of Siglec-1+ thick TNT between HIV-1 infected macrophages persisted for more than one week upon HIV-1 infection (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), suggesting a high degree of stability for these TNT.
evidence: This claim is based on observation shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Siglec-1+ thick TNT have a high degree of stability.
source: In general, we also noticed that the incidence of Siglec-1+ thick TNT between HIV-1 infected macrophages persisted for more than one week upon HIV-1 infection (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), suggesting a high degree of stability for these TNT.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Siglec-1 depletion did not affect the total number of thick TNT.
source: While this depletion did not affect the total number of thick TNT (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), we observed a 2-fold shortening of thick TNT in cells lacking Siglec-1 when compared to control cells (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is based on quantification shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Siglec-1 depletion resulted in a 2-fold shortening of thick TNT.
source: While this depletion did not affect the total number of thick TNT (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), we observed a 2-fold shortening of thick TNT in cells lacking Siglec-1 when compared to control cells (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is based on quantification shown in Figure 4C.

claim: VLP binding was consistently observed along Siglec-1+ thick TNT.
source: We consistently observed binding of VLP along Siglec-1+ thick TNT (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is based on observation shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: In the absence of Siglec-1, there was a significant reduction of VLP binding in comparison to control cells.
source: Yet, in the absence of Siglec-1, we noticed a significant reduction of VLP binding in comparison to control cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is based on quantification shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Blocking monoclonal antibody against Siglec-1 showed that this receptor is involved in HIV-1 binding in cmMTB-treated cells.
source: We confirmed this functional observation using a blocking monoclonal antibody against Siglec-1, showing that this receptor is involved in HIV-1 binding in cmMTB-treated cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is based on blocking experiment shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The siRNA-mediated depletion of Siglec-1 significantly diminished the capacity of cmMTB-treated macrophages to transfer HIV-1 to recipient cells.
source: The siRNA-mediated depletion of Siglec-1 significantly diminished the capacity of cmMTB-treated macrophages to transfer HIV-1 to recipient cells (Figure 4D), indicating that this receptor is involved in the macrophage-to-macrophage viral spread (Souriant et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is based on co-culture experiment shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Siglec-1 is involved in the macrophage-to-macrophage viral spread.
source: The siRNA-mediated depletion of Siglec-1 significantly diminished the capacity of cmMTB-treated macrophages to transfer HIV-1 to recipient cells (Figure 4D), indicating that this receptor is involved in the macrophage-to-macrophage viral spread (Souriant et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an inference based on the data shown in Figure 4D and supported by citation to Souriant et al., 2019.

claim: There was a decreasing tendency for the capacity of Siglec-1-depleted cmMTB-treated macrophages to transfer mitochondria to recipient cells compared to controls.
source: Intriguingly, there was a decreasing tendency for the capacity of Siglec-1-depleted cmMTB-treated macrophages to transfer mitochondria to recipient cells compared to controls (Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1F), alluding to a possible defect in mechanisms involved in intercellular material transfer including through thick TNT (Torralba et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is based on co-culture experiment shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Silencing Siglec-1 expression in cmMTB-treated cells abolished the exacerbation of HIV-1 infection and production.
source: Remarkably, using replicative HIV-1 ADA strain (Figure 4A), we showed that silencing Siglec-1 expression in cmMTB-treated cells abolished the exacerbation of HIV-1 infection and production, as well as the enhanced formation of multinucleated giant cells (MGC) (Figure 4F–G), which are pathological hallmarks of HIV-1 infection of macrophages (Vérollet et al., 2015; Vérollet et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4F–G.

claim: Silencing Siglec-1 expression in cmMTB-treated cells abolished the enhanced formation of multinucleated giant cells (MGC).
source: Remarkably, using replicative HIV-1 ADA strain (Figure 4A), we showed that silencing Siglec-1 expression in cmMTB-treated cells abolished the exacerbation of HIV-1 infection and production, as well as the enhanced formation of multinucleated giant cells (MGC) (Figure 4F–G), which are pathological hallmarks of HIV-1 infection of macrophages (Vérollet et al., 2015; Vérollet et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4F–G.

claim: Multinucleated giant cells (MGC) are pathological hallmarks of HIV-1 infection of macrophages.

claim: TB-induced Siglec-1 expression plays a key part in HIV-1 uptake and efficient cell-to-cell transfer.
source: These results determine that TB-induced Siglec-1 expression plays a key part in HIV-1 uptake and efficient cell-to-cell transfer, resulting in the exacerbation of HIV-1 infection and production in M(IL-10) macrophages.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the data presented in the Results section.

claim: TB-induced Siglec-1 expression results in the exacerbation of HIV-1 infection and production in M(IL-10) macrophages.
source: These results determine that TB-induced Siglec-1 expression plays a key part in HIV-1 uptake and efficient cell-to-cell transfer, resulting in the exacerbation of HIV-1 infection and production in M(IL-10) macrophages.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the data presented in the Results section.

claim: Pulmonary active TB has been characterized as an IFN-I-driven disease.
source: Although pulmonary active TB has been characterized as an IFN-I-driven disease (Berry et al., 2010; McNab et al., 2015; Moreira-Teixeira et al., 2018), there are no report in the literature about a role for Siglec-1 in TB or in Mtb co-infection with retroviruses.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Berry et al., 2010; McNab et al., 2015; Moreira-Teixeira et al., 2018.

claim: There are no reports in the literature about a role for Siglec-1 in TB or in Mtb co-infection with retroviruses.
source: Although pulmonary active TB has been characterized as an IFN-I-driven disease (Berry et al., 2010; McNab et al., 2015; Moreira-Teixeira et al., 2018), there are no report in the literature about a role for Siglec-1 in TB or in Mtb co-infection with retroviruses.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Expression of Siglec-1 is restricted to myeloid cells except circulating monocytes.
source: Expression of Siglec-1 is restricted to myeloid cells except circulating monocytes (Crocker et al., 2007), and is enhanced by IFN-I (Puryear et al., 2013; Rempel et al., 2008) and during HIV-1 infection (Pino et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Crocker et al., 2007.

claim: Siglec-1 expression is enhanced by IFN-I.
source: Expression of Siglec-1 is restricted to myeloid cells except circulating monocytes (Crocker et al., 2007), and is enhanced by IFN-I (Puryear et al., 2013; Rempel et al., 2008) and during HIV-1 infection (Pino et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Puryear et al., 2013; Rempel et al., 2008.

claim: Siglec-1 expression is enhanced during HIV-1 infection.
source: Expression of Siglec-1 is restricted to myeloid cells except circulating monocytes (Crocker et al., 2007), and is enhanced by IFN-I (Puryear et al., 2013; Rempel et al., 2008) and during HIV-1 infection (Pino et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Pino et al., 2015.

claim: Human alveolar macrophages are distinguished from lung interstitial macrophages by Siglec-1 expression.
source: In addition, human alveolar macrophages are distinguished from lung interstitial macrophages by Siglec-1 expression (Yu et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Yu et al., 2016.

claim: IFN-I present in TB-associated environment is responsible for Siglec-1 overexpression in human macrophages.
source: In this study, we determined that IFN-I present in TB-associated environment is responsible for Siglec-1 overexpression in human macrophages, which resembled that obtained in HIV-1-infected cells.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the data presented in the Results section.

claim: IL-10 induces the autocrine production of IFN-I.
source: This could be explained by the fact that IL-10 induces the autocrine production of IFN-I (Ziegler-Heitbrock et al., 2003) to indirectly modulate Siglec-1 expression in M(IL-10) macrophages, which then contributes to the exacerbation of HIV-1 infection as we previously reported (Souriant et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ziegler-Heitbrock et al., 2003.

claim: The in vivo expression of Siglec-1 is up-regulated early in myeloid cells after SIV infection and maintained thereafter in the pathogenic NHP model.
source: This is in line with a recent report on the presence of IFN-I, IFNAR and different ISG in alveolar and lung interstitial tissue from NHP with active TB (Mattila, 2019), and with the fact that the in vivo expression of Siglec-1 is up-regulated early in myeloid cells after SIV infection and maintained thereafter in the pathogenic NHP model (Jaroenpool et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Jaroenpool et al., 2007.

claim: IFN-I is present in alveolar and lung interstitial tissue from NHP with active TB.
source: This is in line with a recent report on the presence of IFN-I, IFNAR and different ISG in alveolar and lung interstitial tissue from NHP with active TB (Mattila, 2019), and with the fact that the in vivo expression of Siglec-1 is up-regulated early in myeloid cells after SIV infection and maintained thereafter in the pathogenic NHP model (Jaroenpool et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Mattila, 2019.

claim: In TB-SIV co-infection, IFN-I is not exerting the expected antiviral effect, but instead is concomitant with chronic immune activation and attenuated by the high expression of Siglec-1 in myeloid cells.
source: In TB-SIV co-infection, we hypothesized that IFN-I is not exerting the expected antiviral effect, but instead is concomitant with chronic immune activation and attenuated by the high expression of Siglec-1 in myeloid cells, as recently proposed in the HIV-1 context (Akiyama et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the data presented and supported by citation to Akiyama et al., 2017.

claim: The IFN-I/STAT1/Siglec-1 axis is a mechanism established by Mtb to exacerbate HIV-1 infection in myeloid cells.
source: Altogether, these findings uncover the IFN-I/STAT1/Siglec-1 axis as a mechanism established by Mtb to exacerbate HIV-1 infection in myeloid cells, and call for the need to further investigate this signaling pathway in TB pathogenesis.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the data presented in the Results section.

claim: No receptor has been described so far to be present mainly on thick TNT.
source: To our knowledge, no receptor has been described so far to be present mainly on thick TNT, making Siglec-1 an unprecedented potential marker for this subtype of TNT (Dupont et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Siglec-1 is an unprecedented potential marker for thick TNT.
source: To our knowledge, no receptor has been described so far to be present mainly on thick TNT, making Siglec-1 an unprecedented potential marker for this subtype of TNT (Dupont et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference based on the data presented and supported by citation to Dupont et al., 2018.

claim: The IFN-I/STAT1 axis is responsible for Siglec-1 expression in M(IL-10) macrophages, but does not contribute to TNT formation.
source: This suggests that, while the IFN-I/STAT1 axis is responsible for Siglec-1 expression in M(IL-10) macrophages, it does not contribute to TNT formation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data presented.

claim: TNT formation induced by TB-associated microenvironments depended on the IL-10/STAT3 axis.
source: This is line with our previous report where TNT formation induced by TB-associated microenvironments depended on the IL-10/STAT3 axis (Souriant et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Souriant et al., 2019.

claim: The shortening of thick TNT length may reflect a fragile state due to an altered cell membrane composition in the absence of Siglec-1.
source: Concerning the shortening of thick TNT length, we infer that it may reflect a fragile state due to an altered cell membrane composition in the absence of Siglec-1; TNT are known for their fragility towards light exposure, shearing force and chemical fixation (Rustom et al., 2004).
evidence: This is an inference based on the data presented and supported by citation to Rustom et al., 2004.

claim: TNT are known for their fragility towards light exposure, shearing force and chemical fixation.
source: Concerning the shortening of thick TNT length, we infer that it may reflect a fragile state due to an altered cell membrane composition in the absence of Siglec-1; TNT are known for their fragility towards light exposure, shearing force and chemical fixation (Rustom et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Rustom et al., 2004.

claim: The longer the TNT is, the more rigidity it requires to be stabilized.
source: We hypothesize that the longer the TNT is, the more rigidity it requires to be stabilized.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: Cholesterol and lipids are known to increase membrane rigidity.
source: Cholesterol and lipids are known to increase membrane rigidity (Redondo-Morata et al., 2012) and are thought to be critical for TNT stability (Lokar et al., 2012; Thayanithy et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Redondo-Morata et al., 2012.

claim: Cholesterol and lipids are thought to be critical for TNT stability.
source: Cholesterol and lipids are known to increase membrane rigidity (Redondo-Morata et al., 2012) and are thought to be critical for TNT stability (Lokar et al., 2012; Thayanithy et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lokar et al., 2012; Thayanithy et al., 2014.

claim: The presence of Siglec-1 in thick TNT may affect the cholesterol and lipid composition via the recruitment of GM1/GM3 glycosphingolipid-enriched microvesicles.
source: Thus, the presence of Siglec-1 in thick TNT may affect the cholesterol and lipid composition via the recruitment of GM1/GM3 glycosphingolipid-enriched microvesicles (Halász et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the data presented and supported by citation to Halász et al., 2018.

claim: TNT formation depends on GM1/GM3 ganglioside and cholesterol content.
source: In fact, TNT formation depends on GM1/GM3 ganglioside and cholesterol content (Kabaso et al., 2011; Lokar et al., 2012; Osteikoetxea-Molnár et al., 2016; Tóth et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kabaso et al., 2011; Lokar et al., 2012; Osteikoetxea-Molnár et al., 2016; Tóth et al., 2017.

claim: GM1 and GM3 glycosphingolipids are bona fide ligands for Siglec-1.
source: Since GM1 and GM3 glycosphingolipids are bona fide ligands for Siglec-1 (Puryear et al., 2013), it is likely that Siglec-1+ thick TNT exhibit a higher lipid and cholesterol content, and hence an increase of membrane rigidity that favors the stability of longer TNT.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Puryear et al., 2013.

claim: Siglec-1+ thick TNT likely exhibit a higher lipid and cholesterol content, and hence an increase of membrane rigidity that favors the stability of longer TNT.

evidence: This is an inference based on the data presented and supported by citation to Puryear et al., 2013.

claim: Infectious synapse and exosome release are mechanisms attributed to Siglec-1 that contribute to cell-to-cell transfer of HIV-1.
source: While infectious synapse and exososome release are mechanisms attributed to Siglec-1 that contribute to cell-to-cell transfer of HIV-1 (Bracq et al., 2018; Gummuluru et al., 2014; Izquierdo-Useros et al., 2014), they accomplish so extracellularly.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bracq et al., 2018; Gummuluru et al., 2014; Izquierdo-Useros et al., 2014.

claim: Siglec-1 participates indirectly in the intracellular HIV-1 transfer via TNT as a tunnel over long distance.
source: Here, we speculate that Siglec-1 participates indirectly in the intracellular HIV-1 transfer via TNT as a tunnel over long distance, suggesting that factors affecting TNT rigidity favor distal viral dissemination while ensuring protection against immune detection.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the data presented.

source: As TNT-transferred mitochondria are known to alter the metabolism and functional properties of recipient cells under steady state conditions or in the cancer context, it implies that Siglec-1 may also influence key metabolic pathways such as glycolysis, pentose phosphate and lipid metabolism, among others (Hekmatshoar et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hekmatshoar et al., 2018.

claim: The gain of cancer drug resistance is directly associated to TNT-mediated mitochondria transfer.
source: This is important because, for example, the gain of cancer drug resistance is directly associated to TNT-mediated mitochondria transfer, thus Siglec-1 may represent a novel therapeutic strategy to overcome cancer cell drug resistance.

claim: The depletion of Siglec-1 abrogated the exacerbation of HIV-1 infection and production induced by TB in M(IL-10) macrophages likely results from an accumulative effect of deficient capture and transfer of HIV-1 in the absence of Siglec-1.
source: Finally, the depletion of Siglec-1 abrogated the exacerbation of HIV-1 infection and production induced by TB in M(IL-10) macrophages. This is likely to result from an accumulative effect of deficient capture and transfer of HIV-1 in the absence of Siglec-1.

claim: A loss-of-function variant in Siglec-1 in the human population does not conclusively establish a role for this receptor in AIDS progression.
source: It is worth noting that we have previously reported that a loss-of-function variant in Siglec-1 in the human population does not conclusively establish a role for this receptor in AIDS progression, even though ex vivo experiments demonstrated that cells from these individuals were functionally null or partially defective for Siglec-1 expression along with poor HIV-1 capture and transmission (Martinez-Picado et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Martinez-Picado et al., 2016.

claim: Cells from individuals with a loss-of-function variant in Siglec-1 were functionally null or partially defective for Siglec-1 expression along with poor HIV-1 capture and transmission.

claim: There are several challenges to the study of Siglec-1 variants, such as limited cohort size, the lack of complete clinical records, and the restriction to study only off-therapy periods.
source: While this may be counterintuitive for proposing Siglec-1 as a therapeutic target to limit viral dissemination in the co-infection context, there are several challenges to the study of Siglec-1 variants, such as limited cohort size, the lack of complete clinical records, and the restriction to study only off-therapy periods, among others (Martinez-Picado et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Martinez-Picado et al., 2017.

claim: Siglec-1 localization on thick TNT has a physiological significance to macrophage biology in health and disease.
source: We argue that Siglec-1 localization on thick TNT has a physiological significance to macrophage biology in health and disease.
